scarcity-s1.title: One empty lot in Riverton
scarcity-s1.html: The town of Riverton (an invented town) owns one empty lot downtown. Residents want a park, store owners want a parking garage, and a grocery chain offers to lease the lot for a new store. Building the garage would take a crew of 40 construction workers, two cranes and a fleet of dump trucks, and a local developer has offered to put up her own savings to run the project.

items.q: What makes the choice about Riverton's lot an economic problem?
options: The town has run out of money for any project
The lot cannot be used for a park, a garage and a store at the same time
Store owners care more than residents do
The grocery chain sets the price of the lease

items.q: Which factor of production is the lot itself?
options: Land
Labor
Capital
Entrepreneurship

items.q: In the garage plan, which item is capital?
options: The 40 construction workers
The empty lot
The developer's willingness to risk her savings
The two cranes and the dump trucks

items.q: The developer offers her own savings to run the garage project. Which factor of production does she supply, and why?
options: Capital, because she provides money
Labor, because she works on the project
Entrepreneurship, because she organizes the project and takes the risk
Land, because the garage sits on the lot

items.q: Which country in the table has a command economy?
options: Lorna
Pavlo
Quill
Lorna and Quill together

items.q: Which country in the table is closest to how most real economies work?
options: Quill, a mixed economy
Lorna, a pure market economy
Pavlo, a pure command economy
Pavlo and Lorna equally

items.q: In Lorna, how is the "for whom" question mostly answered?
options: By government planners assigning goods to each household
By giving each household the same amount
By the order in which people line up
By who is willing and able to pay market prices

items.q: In Pavlo, a factory manager is told to make 500 tractors this year. Which basic question has the government answered?
options: For whom to produce
Whether resources are scarce
What to produce
How much to charge buyers

items.q: Which statement about scarcity is accurate?
options: It ends once a country becomes rich enough
It exists because wants are greater than the resources to meet them
It applies to goods but not to time
It means a store has sold out of a product

items.q: A student has three free hours on Saturday and wants to study, work a paid shift and see friends. What does this show?
options: Scarcity: limited time forces a choice among wants
An economic system answering the question of for whom to produce
A command decision by the student's parents
A factor of production called entrepreneurship

items.q: A city council spends this year's budget on a new bridge, so it repairs fewer school buildings. What is this an example of?
options: A command economy
An increase in resources
A choice with nothing given up
A trade-off

items.q: Which of these are capital in the economic sense? Select all that apply.
options: A delivery van owned by a bakery
A robot arm on a car assembly line
Cash a bakery keeps in its bank account
Crude oil still in the ground

items.q: Which is a service rather than a good?
options: A pair of scissors
A bottle of shampoo
A haircut
A barber's chair

items.q: A country discovers a large new field of natural gas. Which factor of production has it gained more of?
options: Labor
Land
Capital
Entrepreneurship

items.q: A neighbor says, "Scarcity is not a problem for billionaires." What is the best reply?
options: They still face limited time and must choose how to use it and their money
They are right: with enough money each want is met
They are right, at least in a market economy
Scarcity applies to governments, not to people

items.q: Put the steps from scarcity to a decision in order.
options: Wants are greater than the resources available
Resources are scarce
People must choose how to use them
Each choice gives up something else (a trade-off)

items.q: Label this production possibilities curve for an economy that makes pizzas (on the horizontal axis) and robots (on the vertical axis).
A recession leaves many factories idle and many workers without jobs. Place point U to show what the economy produces.
Place point Z at a combination of pizzas and robots the economy cannot produce with its current resources and technology.
Every worker and machine is employed in its best use. Place point F to show one combination the economy could produce.
A new technology raises how much of both goods the economy can make. Show the change on the graph.

key.because: a new technology that raises output of both goods

items.q: A hurricane destroys many factories and farms. Show the change on the graph.

key.because: a hurricane that destroys factories and farms

items.q: Using the table, what is the opportunity cost per million bushels of wheat when Dornia moves from combination 2 to combination 3?

mistakes.why: You divided the wheat gained by the tractors given up. Opportunity cost is what is given up per unit gained: 4 / 10.
That is the total cost of the 10 million bushels. The question asks per million bushels: divide by 10.

items.q: Using the table, how many thousand tractors does Dornia give up in total to move from combination 3 to combination 4?

mistakes.why: That is the number of tractors still made at combination 4. The cost is how many were given up: 14 - 8.
That is the wheat gained. The opportunity cost is measured in the good given up, tractors.

items.q: What does the table show about Dornia's opportunity cost of wheat as it makes more wheat?
options: It stays the same: each extra 10 million bushels costs 2 thousand tractors
It rises: each extra 10 million bushels costs more tractors than the last
It falls: wheat gets cheaper to make as Dornia makes more
It is impossible to find from a table

items.q: Could Dornia produce 25 million bushels of wheat and 14 thousand tractors in the same year?
options: No: that combination lies outside its PPC
Yes: it lies inside its PPC, with resources to spare
Yes: it lies on its PPC
Yes, once it gives up some wheat

items.q: Dornia is producing 20 million bushels of wheat and 10 thousand tractors. What does this tell you?
options: It is producing at an efficient point
It has the best technology in the world
It has just lost a large share of its factories in a hurricane
Some of its resources are unemployed or used inefficiently

items.q: What change could explain the move from the faded curve to the new one in the graph?
options: Bellmark puts its idle factories back to work
The price of machines rises
Bellmark gains more workers and better machines
Bellmark shifts workers from making food to making machines

items.q: A combination of food and machines lay just outside Bellmark's faded curve. Where does it lie now?
options: It is still unattainable, because the whole curve shifted
It may now be attainable, on or inside the new curve
It is now inside the faded curve
It has moved to the horizontal axis

items.q: Bellmark's new curve still bows outward. What does that shape tell you?
options: Resources are not equally good at making food and machines
Each extra unit of food costs the same number of machines
Bellmark has idle resources
Bellmark is unable to make more of both goods

items.q: Jordan's Saturday options, in order of preference, are a hike with friends, a paid work shift worth $80, and studying. If Jordan goes on the hike, what is the opportunity cost?
options: The work shift and the studying, added together
Nothing, because the hike is free
The studying, because it ranks last
The $80 work shift, the next-best choice

items.q: A country's PPC is a straight line from 60 thousand shirts (and no jackets) to 20 thousand jackets (and no shirts). What is the opportunity cost of one jacket, in shirts?

mistakes.why: That is the cost of one shirt in jackets (20 / 60). For a jacket, divide the shirts given up by the jackets gained: 60 / 20.

items.q: An economy spends more of its resources this year on factories and machines and less on consumer goods. What happens to its PPC in the future?
options: It shifts in, because people have fewer consumer goods today
It stays where it is, because total resources are unchanged
It shifts out farther, because the extra capital raises future production
It becomes a straight line

items.q: Why is a production possibilities curve usually bowed outward rather than straight?
options: Each resource is equally good at making both goods
Some resources are better at making one good than the other
The economy has idle resources at each point
Prices rise as output rises

items.q: Using the table, what is Marnovia's opportunity cost of making one hat, in shirts?

mistakes.why: That is the cost of one shirt in hats (8 / 24). For one hat, divide the shirts given up by the hats gained: 24 / 8.

items.q: Which country has the absolute advantage in hats?
options: Delmont, because it has the lower opportunity cost of making hats
Marnovia, because one worker makes 8 hats a day to Delmont's 6
Delmont, because it makes fewer shirts per worker
Neither, because both countries make hats

items.q: Which country has the comparative advantage in hats?
options: Delmont, because a hat costs it 2 shirts and costs Marnovia 3
Marnovia, because each of its workers makes more hats per day
Marnovia, because it makes more of both goods
Delmont, because it makes fewer shirts

items.q: If both countries specialize by comparative advantage, what does each produce?
options: Marnovia makes both, because it is better at both
Marnovia makes hats and Delmont makes shirts
Each makes half of each good
Marnovia makes shirts and Delmont makes hats

items.q: Which terms of trade would benefit both countries?
options: 1 hat for 1.5 shirts
1 hat for 3.5 shirts
1 hat for 2.5 shirts
1 hat for 4 shirts

items.q: Using the table, what is Fenwick's opportunity cost of making one table, in chairs?

mistakes.why: You inverted it, as you would with output data. With hours per unit, a table costs (hours per table) / (hours per chair) = 6 / 2 chairs.

items.q: Which country has the absolute advantage in chairs?
options: Fenwick, because it needs more hours per chair
Ellis, because it needs 1 hour per chair to Fenwick's 2
Fenwick, because it has the lower opportunity cost of chairs
Neither, because both need hours to make chairs

items.q: Which country has the comparative advantage in chairs?
options: Fenwick, because a chair costs it a third of a table and costs Ellis half a table
Ellis, because it needs fewer hours per chair than Fenwick
Ellis, because it is faster at making both goods
Fenwick, because it needs more hours to make a table

items.q: A student says, "Ellis needs fewer hours for both goods, so trade with Fenwick cannot help Ellis." What is wrong with the claim?
options: Nothing: a country with the absolute advantage in both goods gains nothing from trading with others
Ellis gains if Fenwick also has an absolute advantage in something
Trade helps Ellis if it switches to making chairs
Ellis gains by making tables and buying chairs at a price below its own opportunity cost

items.q: A surgeon types faster than her assistant but pays the assistant to do her typing. Which idea explains this?
options: Absolute advantage: the assistant types faster than the surgeon
Scarcity: there is not enough typing to go around
Comparative advantage: the assistant's opportunity cost of typing is lower
Increasing opportunity cost: typing gets harder the more she does

items.q: Can one country have the comparative advantage in both of two goods?
options: Yes: if it has the absolute advantage in both
No: a lower cost of one good means a higher cost of the other
Yes: if it has more workers than the other country
Yes: if its PPC lies farther from the origin

items.q: Two countries specialize by comparative advantage and trade at terms between their opportunity costs. Which results follow? Select all that apply.
options: Their combined output of the two goods can rise
Each can consume a combination outside its own PPC
The country with the absolute advantage in both goods gains and the other loses
Each country's PPC shifts outward

items.q: Two countries have the same opportunity cost of wheat in terms of cloth. What does this imply about trade between them?
options: Neither gains from specializing and trading these goods
Both gain a great deal
The larger country gains and the smaller loses
They gain as long as the terms of trade are set high enough

items.q: Why must mutually beneficial terms of trade lie between the two countries' opportunity costs?
options: The richer country sets the price
Prices in trade are set at the exact average of the two costs
Countries trade goods they are unable to make
Each country must get a good for less than it costs to make at home

items.q: In Marnovia one worker makes 24 shirts or 8 hats a day. Marnovia trades for hats at 1 hat for 2.5 shirts. How many shirts does Marnovia save on each hat it buys instead of making it?

mistakes.why: That is the price Marnovia pays. The gain is its own opportunity cost (3 shirts) minus that price.
That is what a hat costs Marnovia to make. The gain is that cost minus the 2.5 shirts it pays.

items.q: Put the steps for finding comparative advantage from an output table in order.
options: Find each country's opportunity cost of each good
Compare the two countries' opportunity costs for each good
Give each good to the country with its lower opportunity cost
Choose terms of trade between the two opportunity costs

items.q: Buyers' incomes rise, and pizza is a normal good. Shift the right curve the right way in the market for pizza.

key.because: a rise in buyers' incomes for a normal good

slips.S: Income belongs to buyers, so it shifts demand; it does not change pizza makers' costs.

items.q: The price of gasoline rises sharply. Shift the right curve the right way in the market for large, fuel-hungry SUVs.

key.because: a rise in the price of gasoline, a complement

slips.S: Gasoline is used with SUVs by buyers, so its price shifts demand for SUVs, not the supply of SUVs.

items.q: The price of coffee rises. Shift the right curve the right way in the market for tea.

key.because: a rise in the price of coffee, a substitute

slips.S: Coffee's price changes what tea buyers want, so it shifts the demand for tea.

items.q: The price of movie tickets falls and nothing else changes. Place point X where buyers end up on the demand curve.
Incomes in a town rise, and for its residents store-brand instant noodles are an inferior good. Shift the right curve the right way in the market for these noodles.

key.because: a rise in incomes for an inferior good

slips.S: Income belongs to buyers, so it shifts demand, not the noodle makers' supply.

items.q: Which law does the table illustrate?
options: The law of demand: as price rises, demand shifts to the left
The law of demand: as price rises, quantity demanded falls
A direct relationship between price and quantity demanded
A change in demand caused by a change in income

items.q: Using the table, by how many smoothies a day does the quantity demanded fall when the price rises from $3 to $5?

mistakes.why: That is the change in price. The question asks for the change in the quantity demanded: 80 - 40.
You added the two quantities. A change is the difference: 80 - 40.

items.q: The stand raises its price from $4 to $5. How should you describe what happens?
options: Quantity demanded falls from 60 to 40, a movement along the demand curve
Demand decreases, so the demand curve shifts left
Demand increases, because the stand earns more per smoothie
Quantity demanded rises, because the price rose

items.q: A heat wave arrives, and at every price buyers now want 30 more smoothies a day than the table shows. What happened?
options: Quantity demanded increased along the same demand curve
Demand decreased: the curve shifted left
The law of demand stopped holding
Demand increased: the whole demand curve shifted right

items.q: Event (1): gasoline prices jump. What happens to the demand for scooter rides in Hollis?
options: It decreases, because gasoline and scooter rides are complements for riders
The quantity demanded rises along the same curve
It increases, because scooter rides are a substitute for car trips
It does not change, because scooters do not use gasoline

items.q: Event (2): 10,000 students arrive. How does this affect the scooter market?
options: Demand decreases, because students have low incomes
Demand increases, because there are more buyers
Supply increases, because more scooters are needed
Quantity demanded rises because the price falls

items.q: Event (3): riders learn that ride prices will drop sharply next month. What happens to demand for rides this month?
options: It decreases, because riders wait for the lower price
It increases, because riders expect a bargain
It is unchanged until the price of a ride actually falls
The quantity demanded rises along the curve

items.q: Event (4): the company raises its own ride price from $3 to $4. How does the graph of the scooter market show this?
options: A shift of the demand curve to the left
A shift of the demand curve to the right
A movement down along the demand curve to a larger quantity demanded
A movement up along the demand curve to a smaller quantity demanded

items.q: Why does the demand curve slope downward?
options: Sellers offer less at lower prices, so buyers buy less
Buyers' incomes rise whenever a price falls
A lower price lets buyers afford more (income effect) and makes the good cheaper than its alternatives (substitution effect)
A lower price attracts new sellers into the market

items.q: Which pair of goods are complements?
options: Butter and margarine
Hot dogs and hot dog buns
Train tickets and bus tickets
Paper books and e-books

items.q: A student writes, "The price of pizza went up, so the demand for pizza fell." How should the sentence be fixed?
options: "The quantity demanded of pizza fell"; demand itself did not change
"The demand for pizza rose"; higher prices raise demand
"The supply of pizza fell"; prices affect sellers, not buyers
"Demand fell and quantity demanded rose"; both changed

items.q: Make the explanation specific: the price of coffee rises. Fill in each blank to explain what happens in the market for tea.

specific.frame: Coffee's price ___, so some buyers switch to tea because the two are ___, and the demand for tea shifts ___.

change.label: Coffee's price
options: rises
falls

why.1: The scenario says the price of coffee rises.

because.label: How the goods relate
options: substitutes
complements

why.1: Complements are used together; tea replaces coffee, so they are substitutes.

direction.label: Which way demand shifts
options: right
left

why.1: More tea is wanted at every price, a shift right.

specific.model: The price of coffee rises, so some buyers switch to tea because the two are substitutes, and as a result the demand for tea increases: the demand curve shifts right.

items.q: Which events would shift the demand for gasoline-powered cars to the left? Select all that apply.
options: The price of gasoline rises
The price of gasoline-powered cars rises
Buyers' incomes rise, and these cars are a normal good
Many families move into the area

items.q: The price of flour rises. Shift the right curve the right way in the market for bread.

key.because: a rise in the price of flour, an input

slips.D: Flour is an input for bakers, so its price shifts supply; buyers' wants have not changed.

items.q: A new machine lets furniture makers build chairs faster and more cheaply. Shift the right curve the right way in the market for chairs.

key.because: a technology that lowers the cost of making chairs

slips.D: The machine changes what makers can offer, so it shifts supply, not demand.

items.q: The government pays solar panel makers a subsidy for each panel they produce. Shift the right curve the right way in the market for solar panels.

key.because: a subsidy paid to producers for each panel

slips.D: The subsidy goes to producers, so it shifts supply.

items.q: The government starts collecting a tax from producers on every bottle of soda sold. Shift the right curve the right way in the market for soda.

key.because: a tax collected from producers on each bottle

slips.D: The tax is paid by producers, so it shifts supply.

items.q: The market price of honey rises and nothing else changes. Place point X where the farm ends up on its supply curve.
Using the table, by how many jars a week does the quantity supplied rise when the price rises from $6 to $10?

mistakes.why: That is the change in price. The question asks for the change in the quantity supplied: 80 - 40.
You added the quantities. The change is the difference: 80 - 40.

items.q: What does the table show?
options: An increase in supply as the price rises
The law of supply: a higher price brings a larger quantity supplied
An inverse relationship between price and quantity supplied
A shift of the supply curve to the right each time the price changes

items.q: A drought raises the farm's costs, and it now offers 10 fewer jars at every price in the table. What happened?
options: Supply decreased: the supply curve shifted left
Quantity supplied fell along the same supply curve
Supply increased, because honey became scarcer
Demand for honey decreased

items.q: Honey makers expect the price of honey to rise sharply next month. What happens to the supply of honey this month?
options: It increases, because makers rush to produce more honey
The quantity supplied rises along the curve this month
It is unchanged until the price actually rises
It decreases, because makers hold back jars to sell later at the higher price

items.q: Event (1): the price of chips falls by a third. What happens in the smartphone market?
options: Supply decreases, because the chip makers now earn less per chip
Demand increases, because phones get cheaper to buy
Supply increases, because each phone costs less to make
Quantity supplied falls along the supply curve

items.q: Event (2): three new phone makers open factories. What happens to the market supply of phones?
options: It decreases, because existing makers lose customers
It increases, because there are more sellers
It stays the same, because demand did not change
Quantity supplied rises along the curve

items.q: Event (3): a tax of $20 is collected from makers on every phone sold. What happens to the supply of phones?
options: It decreases: the supply curve shifts left
It increases: the supply curve shifts right
The quantity supplied rises along the curve
It is unchanged, because buyers pay the price

items.q: Event (4): a popular video makes buyers want new phones more. Which curve does this event shift?
options: The supply curve, to the right
The supply curve, to the left
Neither curve; it is a movement along supply
The demand curve, to the right

items.q: Why does the supply curve slope upward?
options: Buyers want more at higher prices
Sellers' costs fall as the price rises
A higher price makes it worthwhile for sellers to produce more, even as extra output gets costlier
A higher price attracts more buyers

items.q: A reporter writes, "The price of gasoline rose, so the supply of gasoline increased." How should the sentence be fixed?
options: "The supply of gasoline decreased"; higher prices lower supply
"The quantity supplied of gasoline increased"; supply itself did not change
"The demand for gasoline increased"; price affects buyers
"Supply and quantity supplied both increased"

items.q: Make the explanation specific: the price of flour rises. Fill in each blank to explain what happens in the market for bread.

specific.frame: Flour is ___ for bakers, so its higher price ___ their cost of each loaf, and the supply of bread shifts ___.

because.label: What flour is
options: an input
a substitute

why.1: Bakers use flour to make bread; it is an input, not something buyers choose instead of bread.

change.label: Bakers' cost
options: raises
lowers

why.1: A dearer input makes each loaf cost more to make.

direction.label: Which way supply shifts
options: left
right

why.1: Higher costs mean fewer loaves offered at every price, a shift left.

specific.model: Flour is an input for bakers, so a higher flour price raises the cost of making each loaf, and as a result bakers offer fewer loaves at every price: the supply of bread decreases and shifts left.

items.q: A popular study reports that eating oatmeal is healthy. Shift the right curve in the market for oatmeal and mark the new equilibrium.

key.because: a change in tastes toward oatmeal

slips.S: The study changes what buyers want, so it shifts demand; oatmeal makers' costs are unchanged.

items.q: A drought destroys much of the orange crop. Shift the right curve in the market for orange juice and mark the new equilibrium.

key.because: a drought that raises the cost of oranges, the input

slips.D: The drought changes what juice makers can offer, so it shifts supply, not demand.

items.q: Better robots cut the cost of making bicycles. Shift the right curve and mark the new equilibrium in the bicycle market.

key.because: a technology that lowers the cost of making bicycles

slips.D: Technology changes producers' costs, so it shifts supply.

items.q: The price of hot dogs, a complement, rises sharply. Shift the right curve and mark the new equilibrium in the market for hot dog buns.

key.because: a rise in the price of hot dogs, a complement

slips.S: Hot dogs are bought with buns by buyers, so their price shifts the demand for buns.

items.q: In the market for laptops, buyers' incomes rise (laptops are a normal good) and a new chip lowers the cost of making them. Shift both curves and mark the new equilibrium.

key.because: higher incomes and a lower cost of making laptops

items.q: Using the table, what is the equilibrium price of a cup of cocoa?
Using the table, how large is the shortage at a price of $2?

mistakes.why: You added the two quantities. A shortage is the gap between them: 75 - 45.
You subtracted the wrong way. At a price below equilibrium, quantity demanded is larger, so the shortage is 75 - 45 = 30.

items.q: Using the table, how large is the surplus at a price of $5?

mistakes.why: You added the two quantities. A surplus is the gap between them: 90 - 30.
That is the quantity demanded. The surplus is quantity supplied minus quantity demanded: 90 - 30.

items.q: The fair sets the price of cocoa at $4. What happens next in this market, if the price is free to change?
options: A surplus of 30 cups pushes the price down toward $3
A shortage of 30 cups pushes the price up toward $5
The market stays at $4, because sellers set the price
A surplus of 30 cups pushes the price up

items.q: Cold weather arrives, and buyers now want 30 more cups at every price in the table. What is the new equilibrium price?
Which curve shifted in the graph, and which way?
options: Supply shifted left
Demand shifted right
Supply shifted right
Demand shifted left

items.q: How did the equilibrium change in the graph?
options: The price rose and the quantity rose
The price fell and the quantity rose
The price fell and the quantity fell
The price rose and the quantity fell

items.q: Which event could explain the change in the graph?
options: Several new firms enter the market
The price of a key input rises
Buyers' incomes rise for a normal good
A substitute good becomes cheaper

items.q: What happens to the equilibrium price of blueberries?
options: It falls
It stays the same
It is indeterminate
It rises

items.q: What happens to the equilibrium quantity of blueberries?
options: It rises, because demand increased
It falls, because supply decreased
It is indeterminate without the sizes of the shifts
It stays the same, because the shifts cancel

items.q: What extra information would tell you whether the quantity of blueberries sold rises or falls?
options: Whether the price of blueberries rises or falls
The relative sizes of the demand and supply shifts
How many blueberry growers live in the region
Whether blueberries are a normal or inferior good

items.q: A city holds the price of parking below its equilibrium level. What does the market show?
options: A shortage: drivers want more spaces than are offered
A surplus: more spaces are offered than drivers want
Equilibrium, because the city set the price
A shift of demand to the left

items.q: Make the explanation specific: at the current price, buyers want more of a good than sellers offer. Fill in each blank.

specific.frame: There is a ___, so the price ___; as it does, the quantity demanded ___ and the quantity supplied rises until they are equal.

concept.label: What the market has
options: shortage
surplus

why.1: A surplus means more is offered than wanted; here more is wanted than offered.

price.label: The price
options: rises
falls

why.1: Buyers compete for the scarce units, so the price is bid up, not down.

change.label: Quantity demanded
options: falls
rises

why.1: A higher price lowers the quantity demanded, by the law of demand.

specific.model: There is a shortage, so buyers bid the price up because there are not enough units; as the price rises, the quantity demanded falls and the quantity supplied rises until the two are equal at equilibrium.

items.q: Which events would lower the equilibrium price of wheat, other things equal? Select all that apply.
options: A new seed raises the wheat harvest per acre
A drought cuts the wheat harvest
Bakers want more wheat to meet a rise in bread sales
The price of fertilizer, an input, rises
